operations.anchor: The community’s capacity to help people therefore lives throughout the group instead of inside one professional, guru, or emotionally indispensable founder.
operations.html:
But care is not jurisdiction. The person listening to me should not automatically gain power over my membership, work, housing, children, medicine, or the evidence in a dispute about them. Peer care becomes another hierarchy the moment emotional access turns into administrative authority.

Some things also remain outside peer competence. A community can accompany somebody through grief or conflict and still need a doctor, therapist, child-protection specialist, lawyer, or emergency service. Distributed care is an addition to professional competence, not a magic replacement for it.

operations.anchor: “Your resistance is your wound talking” is one of the most efficient sentences ever invented for avoiding an argument. When a community begins diagnosing dissent instead of responding to it, leave before they schedule a group process about your leaving.
operations.html: There is also a floor the majority cannot vote away: bodily safety, enough food and sleep, independent medical care, private thought, contact with people outside the community, a way to report harm without asking the accused person’s friends for permission, and a usable way to leave. A commune that can democratically abolish these protections is democratic in the same sense that five wolves and a sheep can vote on dinner.

operations.anchor:
Can the community respectfully override the founder?
Can it replace the founder’s role?
Can it revise the founder’s vision?
Can it survive the founder’s absence?
operations.html:
Then follow the boring power. Whose name is on the deed? Who can sign the bank account? Who appoints the bookkeeper, controls records, chooses reviewers, sets admissions, decides access to children or medicine, and can make a complaint disappear? The org chart can say “horizontal” while the keys, passwords, titles, and reputation all point to one person.

An override is real only if it can operate against the person being challenged. If the founder chooses the reviewer, holds the records, owns the land, and can remove the complainant, the community cannot meaningfully override the founder no matter how many circles it holds.

operations.old: A few things help. Judge the method by outcomes people can observe: are members flourishing, can conflicts be resolved, can people disagree safely, and are children doing well? Do not judge it by fidelity to the founder’s preferred interpretation.
operations.new: A few things help. Judge the method by outcomes people can observe: are members flourishing and safe; can conflicts be resolved; can people disagree, leave, and later tell a different story; are children doing well when they grow up; does the community remain materially viable; can it correct a bad prediction; can it replace the founder; and, if it is meant to spread, do later projects actually emerge and last? Longevity, occupancy, consensus, and member retention are not enough by themselves. A prison can score well on several of those metrics. Do not judge the method by fidelity to the founder’s preferred interpretation.

operations.anchor: A community whose children never leave cannot know whether they would freely return. Let them study, travel, make friends, encounter other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
operations.html: Freedom also needs bus fare. Before a child raised in the community is asked to opt into the adult property, work, and governance system, there should be a neutral transition package that makes “no” materially possible: identity documents, portable education or credentials, some savings or launch money, a housing and health bridge, access to records, and help getting somewhere else. This is not a claim that every child owns a proportional slice of the commune. It is a claim that adult consent is fake if the alternative begins with homelessness and zero documents.

operations.new: Keep relationships and a reporting route outside the community.

operations.anchor: Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, and other trusted adults give children perspective and somewhere to speak.
operations.html: At least one trusted adult, advocate, or reporting route should be reachable without going through community leadership.

operations.old: Only a professional faker can hide indefinitely.
operations.new: Even a professional faker can sometimes perform for months; time gives you more evidence, not certainty.

operations.old: At each stage, assess practice and conduct rather than spiritual vocabulary. Vibes are easy. Six months of showing up, listening, repairing harm, and completing ordinary responsibilities is harder to counterfeit.
operations.new: At each stage, assess concrete conduct rather than spiritual vocabulary or therapeutic fluency. Vibes are easy, but so is mistaking conformity for safety. Six months gives you a larger sample; it does not validate a “good person” detector. For high-consequence roles involving children, money, medicine, vehicles, or private records, use conduct-specific evidence, references where appropriate, staged access, and an independent way to challenge the decision.

operations.anchor: • Full membership. Land, money, voice, and long-term obligations follow the founding agreements.
operations.html:
Before provisional membership, do more than hang out. Make one real group decision together, do one ordinary work or money task, and process one small conflict afterward. A premove simulation cannot reveal a soul, but it can reveal whether the actual coordination system works before anybody sells a house.

Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters, and interns do not need full political membership to have rights. If a decision materially affects their pay, schedule, safety, housing, records, or discipline, they need clear terms, a way to be heard, and review. Egalitarianism that stops at the membership boundary can recreate a servant class between communes.

operations.anchor: Rent a meeting space, borrow a room, or use somebody’s home. Discover the group’s conflict capacity before hiring a surveyor.
operations.html: Do the boring capacity budget too: water, housing, food, health care, debt, cash runway, seasonal labor, transport, schooling, market access, and the few skills whose absence can stop everything. A group can have extraordinary emotional skill and still die because the well fails or one exhausted person is the only one who knows the accounts.

operations.anchor: Choose the legal form—cooperative, trust, association, company, or whatever fits the jurisdiction—before the purchase. Decide voting rights, contribution accounting, inheritance, debt, improvements, and what happens when somebody leaves.
operations.html: Then make the finances legible. Members should be able to see current accounts and major obligations; large transfers should need more than one person; conflicts of interest should be disclosed; shared equipment and debts should not live only in the founder’s memory. Define neutral valuation and keep enough liquid reserve that a legitimate exit can actually be paid rather than being a right that activates only when the community has spare cash.

When Somebody Has to Go

A safe community cannot promise to keep everyone. If somebody presents serious or generalized danger, repeatedly violates essential boundaries, or makes ordinary shared life impossible, ejection can be the right answer. Restorative work is useful when it can work on a reasonable timescale; nobody has a duty to turn the commune into a treatment program for a person who is endangering everyone else.

The power to remove somebody is also one of the easiest powers to abuse. Decide the process before the name: what conduct triggers immediate protective action, who preserves evidence, who is recused, who decides temporary restrictions, how the person replies, what review or appeal is possible without endangering others, how housing, money, records, and family contact are protected during separation, and what calls for outside help.

“Outside” does not always mean the nation-state. My research initially leaned too far that way. The important thing is a competent layer that is not reviewing its own conduct: sometimes another community, a federation, a professional, an autonomous regional institution, a court, regulator, or emergency service. The Zapatistas are an important correction here: autonomous institutions can review local power without becoming the state. But autonomy is not permission to ignore law or non-waivable individual rights.

Also choose a mediator or ombud before the crisis. People who have never met the “neutral stranger” until the day of the explosion often do not trust them. Mediation is for repair; it is not a substitute for evidence, safeguarding, adjudication, or a final separation when consent is gone.

operations.old: If the community ends, what happens to the land, debt, buildings, equipment, common funds, and each member’s contributions? What happens to children’s schooling and housing during the transition? Who maintains records? How are unresolved claims handled?
operations.new:
If the community ends, what happens to the land, debt, buildings, equipment, common funds, and each member’s contributions? More immediately: who keeps people housed and fed, gets medications and care to whoever needs them, keeps childcare and schooling going, bridges cash and benefits, provides transport, maintains records and family contact, and takes responsibility for animals and land obligations?

Design this like a living will. Preassign a bridge or successor for each critical function. The institution may be unsalvageable and the people still need breakfast on Tuesday; continuity of basic life should not depend on resurrecting the commune.

operations.anchor: Allow parallel implementations. Fork the method. A community that changes Hearthwork and gets better results has taught me something. If every adaptation still needs the founder’s approval, the parallel versions aren’t really parallel.
operations.html:
Experiment Before You Divorce

And “parallel” does not have to mean everybody buys new land immediately. Try the different rule inside the parent group; then as a semi-autonomous project; then, if it needs more independence, as a nearby seed that still shares selected tools, childcare, business, or friendships. Full fission should be one step on a gradient, not the admission price for experimentation.

Some experiments cannot be tested cheaply. A different land system, population scale, or package of mutually supporting rules may look bad when starved of the assets it actually needs. “We tried it in one room for three months” is not always a fair test.

Federation Without Building Another State

If these communities are supposed to spread, the movement needs infrastructure between them. But the federation should not become one super-commune with a nicer logo.

Pay for the boring layer. The Federation of Egalitarian Communities says it is currently rebuilding. That is a useful warning by itself. Delegates, officer succession, records, compliance, finance, meetings, any dispute functions the federation actually accepts, and a degraded-mode restart plan all consume real labor. If every community gives federation work whatever energy remains after local crises, eventually nothing remains.

Keep it modular. Bilateral friendships and local clusters, function-specific institutions, and the general federation do not all have to be the same organization. The FEC’s PEACH health pool is currently governed independently from FEC delegates. A useful service should be able to survive trouble elsewhere, and a risky financial function should not quietly acquire authority to guarantee everybody else’s debts.

Let cooperation stop short of assimilation. The FEC currently distinguishes full members, communities moving toward membership, and Friends that may choose not to pursue membership. I like that. A stable ally relationship should be allowed to remain a stable ally relationship rather than becoming an unfinished conversion.

Make movement usable, not merely permitted. If somebody can theoretically move between communities but housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes, and transition disputes all fall into cracks, the freedom is mostly decorative. The answer does not have to be one giant harmonized system. Often a thin adapter is enough: define who is responsible for what during the transition and leave the communities’ internal systems alone.

Name what kind of transfer it is. A grant, pooled protection, loan, guarantee, shared-enterprise commitment, reciprocal exchange, and a non-transactional training or relationship visit are not the same economic event. Do not put all of them into one moralized ledger. Solidarity is not unlimited joint liability.

Keep constitutional memory. When a federation hits a hard case—two principles that both seem right until one actual community forces them into conflict—save the facts, competing principles, first judgments, final reasoning, dissent, consequences, and the exact rule version. When the rule changes, rerun the case. Otherwise each generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.

operations.anchor: For the tenth anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders lived with families and learned autonomy by participating in ordinary life. The first sessions brought around 1,500 students, with later sessions bringing thousands more.
operations.html: I also tried to trace what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni continuity, practice transfer, and later organizing; I did not find a clean source chain showing a student went home, founded a directly descended durable commune, and then produced a long-term human-outcome panel. So I’m borrowing a pedagogy and a replication ambition, not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.

operations.old: In 2026, Sénégal increased the punishment for consensual same-sex intimacy to between five and ten years in prison and added penalties for promoting or financing homosexuality. The law comes within the context of an existing reality of arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault, and mob violence—some say prison actually protects homosexuals from the mob. I don’t want to praise communal belonging while ignoring people who survive that belonging by hiding who they are—or by leaving.
operations.new: In March 2026, Sénégal enacted Law No. 2026-08, raising the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to five to ten years in prison. The amended article also criminalizes public “apology” for homosexuality and certain financing or support intended to promote it. The law comes within the context of an existing reality of arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault, and mob violence—some say prison actually protects homosexuals from the mob. I don’t want to praise communal belonging while ignoring people who survive that belonging by hiding who they are—or by leaving.

Research Behind This Article

I did a much larger source audit than would fit comfortably inside the article. The public research report shows the evidence base, limits, counterexamples, and what I still could not verify. It is there so you can inspect the research without turning this article into a 200-row ledger.
